scenario.figure_or_table: Table 2 (vision task parameters) with Section 7.1 methodology and Figure 6 / Section 7.2 results (RT-TAS peak temperature 60.7 C)
scenario.description: Real-time CPUs-GPU thermal-aware scheduling experiment (RT-TAS) on a physical Nvidia Tegra X1 running four automotive vision tasks (feature detector, object tracker, motion estimator, video stabilizer), compared against BASE (Linux CFS) and TEA. The paper publishes per-task CPU/GPU power, execution time and period (Table 2) and a thermal coupling matrix (Table 1). It publishes no floorplan block coordinates or dimensions.
scenario.architecture: Nvidia Tegra X1 SoC with 4 CPU cores and one shared GPU, rated at 15 W maximum, chip thermal resistance 1.15 C/W, fan turned off, per-core thermal sensors, built-in hardware throttling.
scenario.workload: Four periodic vision tasks, each with a 400 ms period, under partitioned fixed-priority scheduling with MPCP GPU locking. Task parameters are in Table 2: feature detector, object tracker, motion estimator and video stabilizer.
scenario.operating_point: CPU and GPU at maximum frequency (CPU 1.7 GHz), temperature threshold 65 C, fan off. Paper observable: maximum transient CPU/GPU core temperature, measured per core by on-chip sensors and aggregated as the peak over cores and time; RT-TAS gives 60.7 C versus TEA 66.7 C and BASE 72.9 C (Figure 6 and Section 7.2).

original_setup.solver: No numerical thermal solver. Temperatures were measured with on-chip per-core sensors on a physical Nvidia Tegra X1 (PDF p.17-18). A lumped core-level RC thermal circuit model, T(t)=TA+R*P+R*C*dT/dt, with an empirically identified 5x5 coupling matrix R (Table 1, PDF p.10), is used for analysis and for the synthetic task-set simulations (PDF p.9-10, 21).
original_setup.optimizer: T-WFD thermally-balanced task-to-core assignment (Algorithm 1, PDF p.13). It is a worst-fit-decreasing heuristic that sorts tasks by non-increasing CPU power times utilization and assigns each to the lowest-temperature feasible core. It is compared against FFD, BFD and WFD.
original_setup.controller: RT-TAS online CPU-GPU co-scheduling (Algorithm 2, PDF p.14). It uses partitioned fixed-priority preemptive scheduling with MPCP GPU locking and bounded priority-inversion budgets. It picks the job whose power best matches the average total power. Compared against BASE (Linux CFS) and TEA. Hardware throttling acts as a fallback above the 65 C threshold.
original_setup.benchmark: Real automotive vision workload on an Nvidia Tegra X1 with 4 CPU cores and a shared GPU (15 W max, chip thermal resistance 1.15 C/W, fan off). Four periodic tasks with 400 ms periods (feature detector, object tracker, motion estimator, video stabilizer), with per-task CPU/GPU power and execution times in Table 2 (PDF p.18). Also 1,000 randomly generated task sets with parameters from Table 3 (PDF p.21).

thermal_observable.location: Maximum temperature among the 4 CPU cores and the GPU, from per-core on-chip thermal sensors on the Tegra X1 (RT-TAS case). Compared with TEA 66.7 C and BASE 72.9 C.
thermal_observable.aggregation: Peak (maximum) transient temperature over all cores and over the experiment time, reported as the core-level peak in Figure 6 and Section 7.2.

physical_mismatches.reason: No floorplan geometry is published: no block x, y, width or height, no die size, no layout coordinates. Fig. 1 is only a qualitative layout schematic. A block-geometry thermal model cannot be built from the paper alone, and no pinned packet asset supplies it.

The original method is a lumped RC thermal-coupling model identified empirically plus real hardware measurement. It is not a spatial 2D or 3D finite-difference/finite-element solver, so a Studio spatial solver would be a different solver class and results cannot be compared numerically with the paper.

The workload is transient and time-varying: periodic jobs, priority inversions and co-scheduling. The published power data are per-task average CPU/GPU power values (Table 2) with no per-block power time series, so a one-row steady power trace would not reproduce the paper's transient dynamics.

The optimizer (T-WFD task-to-core assignment) and the controller (online co-scheduling with inversion budgets, hardware DVFS throttling at 65 C, CPU frequency 1.7 to 0.5 GHz) are scheduling-level mechanisms with no floorplan or placement analog in a thermal Studio.

Real packaging and cooling are not specified in detail: Tegra X1 package, heat spreader, board, passive heat sink and ambient temperature. Only the aggregate chip thermal resistance of 1.15 C/W (from a Nvidia design guide) is given, with the fan off. Thermal-resistance-matrix coefficients (Table 1) are core-level and not material or geometry parameters.

No 3D stacking or interposer is involved. The Tegra X1 is a monolithic 2D SoC, so 3D and interposer mismatches do not apply. Reliability (MTTF, 1.52x lifetime) and cooling-cost ($15.6 per chip) are derived analytically and are not Studio outputs.

assessment.summary: The 2D screening label is not_2d_applicable and Studio did not run (simulation status skipped). The gate failed on input validity: a custom experiment needs 1–128 blocks and a power_w object, but the floorplan and power_w are empty. simulation_allowed is false and comparison_valid is false, so the final verdict is that no Studio result exists. The scenario is a custom 2D steady run, so it has no transient trace, yet the paper's observable is transient. The paper reports a measured peak core temperature of 60.7 C for RT-TAS (TEA 66.7 C, BASE 72.9 C) on a physical Nvidia Tegra X1. This is the maximum over 4 CPU cores and the GPU and over time, taken from on-chip sensors under 400 ms periodic vision tasks, 15 W rating, 1.15 C/W chip resistance, fan off, and a 65 C throttle threshold. No Studio temperature exists, so no numerical comparison is made and nothing here claims replication. Qualitatively, the paper suggests that scheduling and task-to-core placement change peak temperature by several degrees. A spatial 2D model could not test this from the published data, because the scheduling mechanisms have no floorplan analog. No bundled EV6/GCC adaptation or pinned Ascend910/ATPlace placement with generated input.flp and input.ptrace was used, so no source commit or placement assumption applies. The paper links are only a publisher DOI, Linux CFS documentation, and the cpuburn page, and none supplies inputs.
